finalText:
This is a small, dependency-free Node.js HTTP service — five files, no framework, no build step. Here's how it fits together, in request order:

**`server.js`** — entry point. Creates a raw `http.createServer`, calls `verifyToken` on every incoming request's `Authorization` header, rejects with 401 if it fails, otherwise hands `(req, res, user)` off to `route()`. Listens on `PORT` env var (default 8080) when run directly.

**`auth.js`** — bearer token verification. Tokens are `"<userId>.<hexHmacSignature>"`, signed with HMAC-SHA256 using `AUTH_SECRET` (defaults to `'dev-secret'` — worth setting for anything beyond local dev). Uses `crypto.timingSafeEqual` for the comparison, so it's resistant to timing attacks. Note there's no expiry or revocation — a valid token is valid forever as long as the secret doesn't change.

**`routes.js`** — a flat lookup table keyed by `"METHOD /path"` (e.g. `'GET /orders'`) mapping to handler functions. `route()` builds the key from the request, looks up the handler, runs it, and serializes the result as JSON (or 404/500 on failure). Query params are parsed from the URL search string into `q`; POST bodies apparently land in `q.body` too, though I don't see body-parsing middleware in these five files — that's worth double-checking if POST /orders isn't behaving as expected.

**`cache.js`** — a tiny 256-entry in-memory LRU (plain `Map`, reinsert-on-hit to bump recency) sitting in front of reads. No TTL of its own — freshness is delegated to the store.

**`store.js`** — the actual data layer, in-memory (`Map`), standing in for a real database. Every record carries a 15-minute TTL from last write and self-expires on read.

How a request flows, e.g. `GET /orders?id=...`:
`server.js` verifies token → `routes.js` matches `GET /orders` → calls `cached('orders:<userId>', () => listOrders(userId))` → cache miss goes to `store.js`, hit returns from LRU.

One thing to flag since you're new to this: the comment in `routes.js:6` claims writes "invalidate the affected keys," but `POST /orders` → `putOrder()` never actually evicts the `orders:${user.id}` cache entry. So after creating an order, a cached read could keep returning stale data until it falls out of the LRU or the store's 15-minute TTL expires. Worth confirming whether that's a known tradeoff or a real bug.
